msc-21069+3845.name: 61 Cygni
msc-21069+3845.introduction: is a pair of orange dwarfs about 11.4 light-years away in Cygnus, and the first star beyond the Sun whose distance was ever measured. Shining at magnitudes 5.2 and 6.0, the pair is visible to the unaided eye from dark rural skies.

sections.title: The first measured distance to a star
sections.text: In 1838, Friedrich Bessel measured the tiny annual shift of 61 Cygni against the background stars and found a distance of about 10.4 light-years, close to the modern 11.4. It was the first reliable distance to any star other than the Sun, published just before similar measurements of Vega and Alpha Centauri.

sections.title: Piazzi’s Flying Star
sections.text: Giuseppe Piazzi noticed its unusually fast motion by comparing his observations with James Bradley’s from 40 years earlier, and in 1804 he published it as the “Flying Star.” It still has the highest proper motion of any star visible to the unaided eye.

sections.title: Two slow orange suns
sections.text: The two stars orbit each other every 659 years, their separation swinging between about 44 and 124 AU. Since 1943, A has served as the anchor star for class K5 V in the standard system of stellar classification. Both have magnetic cycles, about 7.5 years for A and 11.7 years for B, and B flares more often.

sections.title: Planets claimed, a giant suspected
sections.text: Twentieth-century claims of massive planets, starting in 1942, all proved unfounded; one inspired the planet Mesklin in Hal Clement’s 1953 novel Mission of Gravity. Hipparcos and Gaia measurements now hint at a real giant: a 2026 analysis found the data consistent with a candidate about 8 times Jupiter’s mass, roughly 8 AU from one of the two stars.

procyon.name: Procyon
procyon.introduction: is the brightest star in Canis Minor and usually the eighth-brightest in the night sky, about 11.5 light-years away. Its light comes mainly from Procyon A, a white star nearing the end of its hydrogen-burning life; its companion, Procyon B, is a faint white dwarf.

sections.title: A star on the verge of change
sections.text: Procyon A has 1.5 times the Sun’s mass and gives off seven times as much light. It has nearly exhausted the hydrogen in its core and is evolving into a subgiant. Within roughly 10 to 100 million years it should swell to 80 to 150 times its current diameter.

sections.title: A companion predicted before it was seen
sections.text: As with Sirius, Friedrich Bessel inferred an unseen companion from Procyon’s motion in 1844. John Martin Schaeberle finally saw it in 1896 with the 36-inch refractor at Lick Observatory. Procyon B has only 0.6 solar masses, yet is larger than the heavier Sirius B. The pair orbit every 40.8 years, between about 9 and 21 AU apart.

sections.title: Before the dog
sections.text: The name means “before the dog” in Greek: from northern latitudes Procyon rises before Sirius, the Dog Star. With Sirius and Betelgeuse it forms the Winter Triangle. Procyon appears on the flag of Brazil, representing the state of Amazonas, and the Inuit knew it as Sikuliarsiujuittuq, “the one who never goes onto the newly formed sea ice.”

sections.title: The view from next door
sections.text: Procyon’s nearest neighbor, Luyten’s Star, is only about 1.1 light-years away. From there, Procyon would blaze at magnitude −4.7, brighter than Venus appears to us. From Procyon, the Sun would be an unremarkable magnitude 2.6 star in Aquila.

gj-725.name: Struve 2398
gj-725.introduction: is a pair of red dwarfs about 11.5 light-years away in Draco, also known as Gliese 725 or HD 173739 and HD 173740. Each of its two stars has a known planet.

sections.title: A double from Struve’s catalog
sections.text: It is number 2398 in Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve’s catalog of double stars, sometimes written Σ 2398. Each star has about a third of the Sun’s mass and radius, and they orbit each other every 871 years at about 63 AU apart. Both are X-ray sources, and both are too faint to see without a telescope.

sections.title: A planet for each star
sections.text: A super-Earth of at least 2.8 Earth masses, announced in 2024, circles A every 11 days, too close to be temperate. B has a super-Earth announced in 2025 that orbits within its habitable zone every 37.9 days, and a suspected second planet on a 4.8-day orbit.

gj-15.name: Groombridge 34
gj-15.introduction: is a wide pair of red dwarfs about 11.6 light-years away in Andromeda, also called GJ 15. Its brighter star hosts one of the longest-period Neptune-mass planets known.

sections.title: A circumpolar catalog entry
sections.text: The system was entry 34 in Stephen Groombridge’s catalog of circumpolar stars, published in 1838. Both stars are flare stars, named GX and GQ Andromedae, and they orbit about 93 AU apart, taking around 1,065 years per circuit. The pair passed closest to the Sun about 15,000 years ago and is now receding.

sections.title: Two planets around A
sections.text: A planet of at least 3 Earth masses on an 11.4-day orbit was reported in 2014. A later study failed to detect it but proposed a second, distant planet; longer observations then recovered both. The outer planet, with at least 36 Earth masses, takes about 7,600 days, nearly 21 years, to orbit.

10pc-0039.name: DX Cancri
10pc-0039.introduction: is a tiny red dwarf about 11.7 light-years away, the 18th-closest star system to the Sun and the nearest star in Cancer. At magnitude 14.8, it needs a telescope of at least 40 cm aperture to be seen.

sections.title: A small, flaring star
sections.text: Bjørn Ragnvald Pettersen discovered its variability in 1981, and it was named DX Cancri in 1985. Its unpredictable flares can make it up to five times brighter. It has about 10% of the Sun’s mass, 12% of its radius and a surface temperature of about 2,840 K.

sections.title: A young traveling group?
sections.text: It is a proposed member of the Castor Moving Group, stars that share a common path through space and may have formed together about 200 million years ago.

msc-22034-5647.name: Epsilon Indi
msc-22034-5647.introduction: is a nearby family about 12 light-years away in Indus: the orange dwarf Epsilon Indi A, a cold giant planet, and a distant pair of brown dwarfs, Ba and Bb. A is faintly visible to the unaided eye.

sections.title: A naked-eye star in a hurry
sections.text: Epsilon Indi A has about three-quarters of the Sun’s mass. Its proper motion is the third-highest of any naked-eye star, after Groombridge 1830 and 61 Cygni, and around 2640 it will cross into the neighboring constellation Tucana. From Epsilon Indi, the Sun would appear as a 2.6-magnitude star near the bowl of the Big Dipper.

sections.title: Twin brown dwarfs
sections.text: A brown dwarf companion announced in January 2003 turned out by August to be two. Ba and Bb, of about 47 and 28 Jupiter masses, orbit each other roughly every 15 years, far from A. With temperatures of about 1,300 K and 900 K, they are a benchmark pair for comparing brown dwarf atmospheres.

sections.title: A cold giant seen by Webb
sections.text: Webb imaged the giant planet Epsilon Indi Ab in 2023, detecting its own mid-infrared glow. It is several times Jupiter’s mass, the closest known planet more massive than Jupiter, and at about 2 °C it is one of the coldest exoplanets ever imaged directly. It also surprised astronomers: it is about twice as massive and a little farther from its star than predicted.

source.title: NASA: Webb images cold exoplanet 12 light-years away

sections.title: A SETI favorite
sections.text: In 1972, the Copernicus satellite examined Epsilon Indi for ultraviolet laser signals, without result. It tops a list of 17,129 nearby stars judged most likely to host planets able to support complex life, compiled by Margaret Turnbull and Jill Tarter.

10pc-0044.name: Tau Ceti
10pc-0044.introduction: is the closest solitary Sun-like star, about 11.9 light-years away in Cetus. Easily visible at magnitude 3.5, it has about 78% of the Sun’s mass, fewer heavy elements and probably about twice the Sun’s age, which has long made it a favorite target in the search for life.

sections.title: Listening for neighbors
sections.text: In 1960, Frank Drake chose Tau Ceti and Epsilon Eridani as the first targets of Project Ozma, a radio search for signals from other civilizations. Some 200 hours of listening found nothing, but Tau Ceti has stayed on SETI target lists ever since.

sections.title: A dusty, bombarded system
sections.text: In 2004, astronomers found more than ten times as much cometary and asteroidal material around Tau Ceti as around the Sun, in a belt mostly 35–50 AU from the star. Any planets would be struck by large impacts roughly ten times as often as Earth is today.

sections.title: Planets still in question
sections.text: Candidate planets have been proposed since 2012, including Tau Ceti e and f near the habitable zone, but as of 2025 none is unambiguously confirmed. The star appears almost pole-on, so planets in matching orbits could be considerably more massive than their minimum masses suggest.

sections.title: A star in fiction
sections.text: Tau Ceti is a setting in Andy Weir’s 2021 novel Project Hail Mary and its 2026 film adaptation, where the hypothetical planet Tau Ceti e is called Adrian. The 2026 video game Directive 8020 centers on another hypothetical world, Tau Ceti f.

10pc-0045.name: GJ 1061
10pc-0045.introduction: is a small, quiet red dwarf about 12 light-years away in Horologium. It hosts three rocky planets, two of them in or near its habitable zone.

sections.title: Closer than it looked
sections.text: Its large motion was known by 1974, but its distance was first estimated at about 25 light-years. In 1997 the RECONS team measured it at roughly half that, making it the 20th-nearest known star system at the time.

sections.title: Three small worlds
sections.text: The Red Dots project announced three planets in 2019, each with less than twice Earth’s mass. GJ 1061 c, with a 6.7-day year, orbits near the inner edge of the habitable zone; d, with a 13-day year, lies within it. As of 2025 they are the third- and fourth-nearest known rocky planets in a habitable zone, after Proxima Centauri b and Ross 128 b.

sections.title: A calm host
sections.text: The star is at least 7 billion years old, rotates only once in about 125 days and does not flare noticeably. That calm improves the chances that its planets have kept any atmospheres they had.

10pc-0049.name: YZ Ceti
10pc-0049.introduction: is a faint red dwarf about 12 light-years away in Cetus with three small planets on very tight orbits. It lies only about 1.6 light-years from Tau Ceti.

sections.title: Years measured in days
sections.text: The three planets, announced in 2017, complete their orbits in roughly two to five days, far too close to the star for a temperate climate. Their estimated equilibrium temperatures range from below freezing to more than 200 °C.

sections.title: A planetary magnetic field?
sections.text: Two 2023 studies detected radio bursts probably caused by the innermost planet, YZ Ceti b, interacting with the star’s magnetic field. It may be the first detection of a magnetic field generated by a rocky exoplanet.

sections.title: A flare star
sections.text: Like many red dwarfs, YZ Ceti flares unpredictably, and starspots make it vary slightly as it rotates, about once every 68 days.

10pc-0053.name: Luyten’s Star
10pc-0053.introduction: is a red dwarf about 12.3 light-years away in Canis Minor, also known as GJ 273. It lies only about 1.2 light-years from Procyon, and its planet GJ 273 b is one of the closest known worlds in a habitable zone.

sections.title: Procyon in its sky
sections.text: From Luyten’s Star, Procyon would shine at magnitude −4.5, as bright as Venus at its best in our sky. The two stars passed closest, about 1.12 light-years apart, roughly 600 years ago. Willem Luyten and Edwin Ebbighausen first measured its large motion in 1935.

sections.title: Two planets and two candidates
sections.text: GJ 273 b, discovered in 2017, has at least 2.9 Earth masses and an 18.6-day orbit, receiving about as much starlight as Earth. The inner planet, c, orbits in 4.7 days. Two more candidates were reported in 2019.

sections.title: A message sent
sections.text: In October 2017, the project “Sónar Calling GJ 273b” beamed radio signals toward the star from Norway, including a tutorial on decoding them and 33 pieces of music; a second batch followed in 2018. A reply could arrive no earlier than 2042.

10pc-0056.name: Teegarden’s Star
10pc-0056.introduction: is a tiny red dwarf about 12.5 light-years away in Aries, with only about 9% of the Sun’s mass. Although it moves about 5 arcseconds a year across the sky, it was not found until 2003, and it hosts at least three Earth-mass planets.

sections.title: Found in an asteroid archive
sections.text: A team led by NASA astrophysicist Bonnard Teegarden found it by mining old images from the Near-Earth Asteroid Tracking program, without direct access to a telescope of their own. The star was later found on photographic plates taken in 1951.

sections.title: Briefly the third-nearest star
sections.text: Its first parallax would have put it only 7.5 light-years away, the third-nearest star system known at the time. Its oddly low brightness for that distance hinted at an error, and a 2009 measurement placed it at about 12.6 light-years.

sections.title: Three small planets
sections.text: In 2019, the CARMENES survey found two Earth-mass planets: b orbits in the optimistic habitable zone, like a world between Venus and Earth, and c near its outer edge, like Mars. A 2024 study added d, on a 26-day orbit, with temperatures like those of Jupiter’s icy moons.

sections.title: Watching Earth transit
sections.text: The planets do not pass in front of their star as seen from Earth. The reverse is different: from 2044 to 2496, observers at Teegarden’s Star could see Earth transit the Sun.

10pc-0059.name: Kapteyn’s Star
10pc-0059.introduction: is a red subdwarf about 12.8 light-years away in Pictor and the nearest halo star to the Sun, a member of the Milky Way’s ancient population. At magnitude 8.8, it is visible in binoculars.

sections.title: The star that vanished from its spot
sections.text: In 1898, Jacobus Kapteyn noticed that a catalogued star seemed to be missing; Robert Innes found an uncatalogued star about 15 arcseconds away. It was moving more than 8 arcseconds a year, the highest proper motion then known, until Barnard’s Star took the record in 1916.

sections.title: An ancient outsider
sections.text: Kapteyn’s Star orbits the Milky Way in the opposite direction to most nearby stars and has only about 14% of the Sun’s abundance of heavy elements. Roughly 11 billion years old, it may once have belonged to Omega Centauri, the probable core of a dwarf galaxy swallowed by the Milky Way.

sections.title: Planets that did not hold up
sections.text: Two planets announced in 2014 included what was billed as the oldest known potentially habitable world, and the announcement came with a science-fiction story by Alastair Reynolds. A 2021 analysis showed that both signals came from the star’s rotation and activity.

10pc-0060.name: Lacaille 8760
10pc-0060.introduction: is the brightest red dwarf in Earth’s night sky, about 12.9 light-years away in Microscopium. At magnitude 6.7 it lies at the limit of naked-eye visibility and can be glimpsed only under exceptionally dark skies.

sections.title: From Lacaille’s southern survey
sections.text: Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille recorded it while observing from the Cape of Good Hope; his catalog was published in 1763, after his death. The number 8760 comes from Francis Baily’s 1847 edition of the catalog.

sections.title: A large red dwarf
sections.text: With about 60% of the Sun’s mass and half its radius, it is one of the largest red dwarfs known, classified anywhere from K7 to M2 over the years. Patrick Byrne discovered its mild flares in 1979, earning it the name AX Microscopii. Its expected lifetime, about 75 billion years, is seven times the Sun’s.

kruger-60.name: Krüger 60
kruger-60.introduction: is a pair of red dwarfs about 13 light-years away in Cepheus that orbit each other every 45 years. The pair is approaching and will pass about 6.4 light-years from the Sun in some 88,600 years.

sections.title: Number 60 on a list of doubles
sections.text: Adalbert Krüger flagged it as a possible double star in an 1890 catalog. Sherburne Wesley Burnham examined 67 of his candidates, and number 60 on that list gave the system its name.

sections.title: A flaring partner
sections.text: A has about 27% of the Sun’s mass and B about 18%. In 1951, Peter van de Kamp and Sarah Lee Lippincott found that B is a flare star, now called DO Cephei; flares lasting as long as an hour have been recorded.

scr-j1845-6357.name: SCR J1845−6357
scr-j1845-6357.introduction: pairs one of the smallest and coolest known stars with a brown dwarf, about 13 light-years away in Pavo. It is the closest known red dwarf–brown dwarf binary.

sections.title: A tiny star
sections.text: SCR 1845−6357 A has about 7% of the Sun’s mass, a surface temperature near 2,400 K and only 0.03% of the Sun’s luminosity. At magnitude 17.4, it went unnoticed until the SuperCOSMOS survey found it in 2004.

sections.title: A methane-rich companion
sections.text: Its brown dwarf companion, found in 2006 about 4.1 AU from the star, is a T dwarf of 25 to 65 Jupiter masses with a temperature of about 1,000 K. It is smaller than Jupiter, and like other T dwarfs its spectrum is shaped by methane.

10pc-0065.name: DENIS J1048−3956
10pc-0065.introduction: is a tiny ultracool red dwarf about 13.2 light-years away in Antlia, close to the boundary between the smallest stars and brown dwarfs. At magnitude 17 it can be seen only with a telescope and camera, and it went unrecognized until 2000.

sections.title: Found in an infrared survey
sections.text: Xavier Delfosse, Thierry Forveille and colleagues identified it in 2000 in data from the DENIS infrared survey. Its motion shows that it belongs to the young thin disk of the Milky Way.

sections.title: A powerful radio flare
sections.text: Radio observations reported in 2005 caught a dramatic flare, showing that even an object with such a cool atmosphere can sustain an energetic magnetic environment.

source.title: Burgasser & Putman 2005: Radio emission and a spectacular flare from DENIS 1048−3956

ross-614.name: Ross 614
ross-614.introduction: is a close pair of red dwarfs about 13.4 light-years away in Monoceros, also called V577 Monocerotis. Its faint companion was inferred from the primary’s wobble long before anyone saw it.

sections.title: Predicted, then seen
sections.text: Frank Elmore Ross discovered the star’s motion in 1927 at Yerkes Observatory. In 1936, Dirk Reuyl detected a wobble revealing an unseen companion. Sarah Lippincott predicted its position in 1951, and Walter Baade used those calculations to resolve the pair for the first time with the new 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar.

sections.title: A featherweight partner
sections.text: The two stars orbit every 16.6 years, about 4 AU apart. A 2022 study found that the companion has only about 95 Jupiter masses, close to the minimum for a true star, and at magnitude 14 it is easily lost in the primary’s glare.

10pc-0068.name: UGPS J0722−0540
10pc-0068.introduction: is a cold T-type brown dwarf about 13 light-years away in Monoceros, the second-closest isolated substellar object known after WISE 0855−0714. Its temperature is only about 500 K, and its mass may be low enough to count as a free-floating planet.

sections.title: Found by its motion
sections.text: Philip Lucas discovered it in UKIDSS images, and its discovery was announced in 2010. First reported at only about 9.5 light-years, which would have placed it among the ten nearest objects to the Sun, it was later found to be about 13 light-years away.

sections.title: Conditional physical estimates
sections.text: Its bolometric luminosity is about 0.00000063 times the Sun’s. At assumed ages of 1 and 5 billion years, evolutionary models give 502/539 K, 10.7/25.8 Jupiter masses and 1.0192/0.886 Jupiter radii, respectively. The displayed ranges connect these scenarios; age is unmeasured.

source.title: Dupuy & Kraus 2013, Science 341, 1492, Table S5

sections.title: Sources: adopted radial velocity
sections.text: Hood et al. (2023) obtain 35.80 −0.15/+0.16 km/s from FIRE spectroscopy. Star View adopts this velocity with a conservative ±0.16 km/s uncertainty. Their unphysically small fitted radius and dependent mass and temperature are withheld.

source.title: Hood et al. (2023): preferred FIRE retrieval and section 4.2

sections.title: Sources: earlier velocity analysis
sections.text: Bochanski et al. (2011) reported 46.9 ± 2.5 km/s from the same spectrum. This alternative is retained, not adopted; the disagreement does not establish changing velocity.

source.title: Bochanski et al. (2011): FIRE spectroscopy

sections.title: Infrared photometry
sections.text: JWST measured F480M = 12.016 ± 0.011 Vega mag on April 17, 2023; visual V remains unavailable.

source.title: Albert et al. (2025), Table 2
Dupuy & Kraus (2013): luminosity and evolutionary scenarios

10pc-0069.name: Wolf 1061
10pc-0069.introduction: is a red dwarf about 14 light-years away in Ophiuchus with three known planets. One of them, Wolf 1061 c, is among the closest potentially habitable planets known.

sections.title: Three planets in old data
sections.text: Max Wolf catalogued the star in 1919. In 2015, a University of New South Wales team found three planets in ten years of archived HARPS observations, with orbits of about 4.9, 17.9 and 67 days. A 2017 reanalysis confirmed b and c but found d more massive, on a larger and more eccentric orbit.

sections.title: On the edge of habitability
sections.text: Wolf 1061 c, a super-Earth, orbits near the inner edge of a habitable zone that extends only about 0.1–0.2 AU from the star. Only Proxima b, Ross 128 b and Luyten b are closer among potentially habitable planets. Its size is unknown, as no transits have been seen.

10pc-0073.name: van Maanen’s Star
10pc-0073.introduction: is the nearest solitary white dwarf, about 14 light-years away in Pisces. Adriaan van Maanen discovered it in 1917.

source.title: Carnegie Science: A 1917 spectrum records evidence of an exoplanetary system

sections.title: A century-old clue to planetary debris
sections.text: A Mount Wilson spectrum from 1917 recorded calcium and other heavy elements in its atmosphere. These should sink below the surface, so their presence points to replenishment by rocky debris: evidence of extrasolar planetary material recorded decades before exoplanets were recognized. It did not identify an individual planet.

sections.title: Before it became a white dwarf
sections.text: A 2008 evolutionary study estimated a progenitor about 2.6 times the Sun’s mass, with a main-sequence lifetime of roughly 900 million years. Its giant phase may have expanded to a radius of roughly 4.6 AU. The model gives about 3.2 billion years of subsequent cooling and a total age near 4.1 billion years. These are model estimates, not direct measurements.

source.title: Burleigh et al. (2008): the DODO survey of van Maanen’s star

wolf-424.name: Wolf 424
wolf-424.introduction: is a pair of very small red dwarfs about 14.4 light-years away in Virgo, between Epsilon and Omicron Virginis. Together they shine at only magnitude 12.5.

sections.title: A photographic double
sections.text: In 1941, Dirk Reuyl noticed that the star looked slightly elongated on photographs: it was two stars. They orbit every 15.5 years, about 4.1 AU apart, with masses of only 0.14 and 0.13 times the Sun’s.

sections.title: Twin flare stars
sections.text: In 1967 both were found to be flare stars, together designated FL Virginis. Their flare activity seems to rise and fall over periods of several years.

10pc-0076.name: Gliese 1
10pc-0076.introduction: is a red dwarf about 14.2 light-years away in Sculptor, also listed as HD 225213. It is number one in two major catalogs of nearby stars, though not because it is especially close.

sections.title: First on the list
sections.text: In the 1950 coordinate system it lies very near the starting point of right ascension, so it came first in both the Gliese Catalogue of Nearby Stars and the Luyten Half-Second catalog. Benjamin Gould documented its large proper motion in 1885.

sections.title: A runaway on a stretched orbit
sections.text: It moves at about 111 km/s relative to its neighbors, fast enough to count as a runaway star. Its eccentric orbit carries it between about 3.5 and 9.2 kiloparsecs from the galactic center; the Sun is about 8.5 kiloparsecs out.

10pc-0077.name: TZ Arietis
10pc-0077.introduction: is a small red dwarf about 14.6 light-years away in Aries, also known as GJ 83.1 and GJ 9066. William Kunkel identified it as a flare star in 1968, and despite its low mass it hosts a giant planet.

sections.title: A giant around a tiny star
sections.text: A giant planet on an eccentric orbit of about 771 days was confirmed in 2020 and independently in 2022. Finding such a substantial companion around a star with only a small fraction of the Sun’s mass challenges simple expectations about planet formation.

source.title: NASA Exoplanet Archive: GJ 9066, confirmed and refuted signals

sections.title: One planet, two names
sections.text: The NASA Exoplanet Archive calls the planet GJ 9066 c, while the 2022 CARMENES study named it TZ Ari b. Earlier candidates did not survive: a 2-day signal came from the star’s rotation, and CARMENES found no evidence for a 240-day planet.

10pc-0080.name: GJ 687
10pc-0080.introduction: is a red dwarf about 14.8 light-years away in Draco with two Neptune-mass planets. Older texts call it Argelander Oeltzen 17415.

sections.title: Two Neptune-mass planets
sections.text: Gliese 687 b, announced in 2014, has at least 18 Earth masses and a 38-day orbit within the star’s habitable zone. A second Neptune-mass planet was found in 2020 on a wider and much colder orbit.

10pc-0082.name: GJ 674
10pc-0082.introduction: is a red dwarf about 14.9 light-years away in Ara, orbited by a close-in planet discovered with HARPS in 2007. The planet completes a year in about 4.7 days.

sections.title: Spots can imitate planets
sections.text: The discovery team had to separate the planet’s 4.7-day signal from a longer one caused by starspots rotating with the star, which turns about every 33 days.

sections.title: A big flare from a quiet star
sections.text: GJ 674 is only weakly active, yet in 2018 it produced a hot ultraviolet flare lasting a few hours. It may belong to the Castor stream, a group of stars thought to be about 200 million years old.

10pc-0084.name: WISE 1639−6847
10pc-0084.introduction: is a cold Y-type brown dwarf about 15.5 light-years away in Triangulum Australe, the second-closest Y dwarf known as of 2024 and the nearest star or brown dwarf in its constellation.

sections.title: A peculiar spectrum
sections.text: C. G. Tinney and colleagues discovered it in WISE data in 2012. Hubble spectra later revealed unusual infrared colors, earning it the class Y0 pec, for peculiar. Atmosphere models can reproduce its spectrum only with an unrealistically high temperature and low gravity.

sections.title: Model estimates from infrared light
sections.text: Fontanive et al. (2023) infer 361 ± 14 K, 13 ± 4 Jupiter masses and log₁₀(L/L☉) = −6.82 ± 0.05. Their ATMO 2020 estimates assume a population age distribution of 5 ± 3 billion years; that is not a measured age. Radius is derived from the same temperature and luminosity.

source.title: Fontanive et al. (2023): HST photometry and evolutionary estimates

sections.title: Infrared measurements
sections.text: Hubble measured F127M = 20.00 ± 0.02 Vega mag in 2019. JWST measured F480M = 13.487 ± 0.005 in 2023. Infrared magnitudes cannot supply visual V.

source.title: Albert et al. (2025), Tables 2 and 4; Fontanive et al. (2023), Tables 2–3
Fontanive et al. (2023): HST photometry and evolutionary estimates

10pc-0085.name: LP 731−58
10pc-0085.introduction: is a very faint red dwarf about 14.9 light-years away in Sextans, also known as LHS 292 and GJ 3622. Seeing it requires a large amateur telescope.

sections.title: An inconspicuous flare star
sections.text: Its late M-type spectrum places it among the coolest nearby red dwarfs. Although its normal light is extremely weak, it can suddenly brighten in magnetic flares.

10pc-0086.name: LAWD 37
10pc-0086.introduction: is a white dwarf about 15.1 light-years away in Musca, also called LP 145−141, and the fourth-closest white dwarf known. In 2019 it became the first solitary white dwarf to have its mass measured directly, by watching it bend the light of a background star.

sections.title: Weighed by bending starlight
sections.text: In 2019 it passed almost in front of a distant star. Hubble measured the tiny shift in that star’s apparent position as LAWD 37’s gravity bent its light. The 2023 analysis found a mass of 0.56 ± 0.08 times the Sun’s.

source.title: NASA: Hubble directly measures the mass of a lone white dwarf

sections.title: A carbon-rich remnant
sections.text: LAWD 37 shows carbon in its spectrum, a rare type called DQ. It has about 1.4 times Earth’s radius and has been cooling for about 1.2 billion years. It is what remains of a B-type star of about 4.4 solar masses.

sections.title: A test of dense matter
sections.text: Combining the gravitational mass with the white dwarf’s radius tests the predicted mass–radius relation. In a white dwarf, adding mass makes the remnant smaller, because its internal support comes from electron degeneracy.

source.title: McGill et al. (2023): testing the white dwarf mass–radius relation
McGill et al. (2023): weighing LAWD 37 through astrometric microlensing

gj-1245.name: GJ 1245
gj-1245.introduction: is a triple system of very small red dwarfs about 15.2 light-years away in Cygnus, also called V1581 Cygni. The largest of the three has only 12% of the Sun’s mass.

sections.title: Two scales of orbit
sections.text: A and C form a close pair about 2 AU apart; C has only 8% of the Sun’s mass. B circles them about 27 AU out, taking an estimated 279 years. The letters can mislead: the tight pair is A–C, not A–B.

sections.title: Flaring siblings
sections.text: A and B are both active flare stars. Stars formed together like these let astronomers compare rotation and magnetic activity close to the minimum mass for hydrogen fusion.

10pc-0090.name: WISE 1741+2553
10pc-0090.introduction: is a very cool T9 brown dwarf about 15 light-years away in Hercules. Its extremely weak visible light hid this neighbor until WISE’s infrared survey revealed it.

sections.title: Discovered three times
sections.text: Three teams published its discovery independently in 2011, all using WISE data with infrared follow-up. Keck adaptive-optics images showed no close companion, so it appears to be a single brown dwarf.

10pc-0091.name: Gliese 876
10pc-0091.introduction: is a red dwarf about 15.2 light-years away in Aquarius, also called IL Aquarii, with four known planets. Its three outer planets move in a rare Laplace resonance, the same rhythm that links Jupiter’s moons Io, Europa and Ganymede.

sections.title: A giant-planet milestone
sections.text: On June 23, 1998, two teams independently announced Gliese 876 b, about twice Jupiter’s mass, showing that a red dwarf could host a giant planet. Planets c, d and e followed in 2001, 2005 and 2010.

sections.title: A celestial rhythm
sections.text: Planets c, b and e take about 30, 61 and 124 days to orbit, close to a 1:2:4 pattern. Their strong mutual tugs change the orbits noticeably over time, which let astronomers measure the system’s architecture and show that the orbits lie almost in one plane.

sections.title: Giants in the habitable zone
sections.text: Planets b and c are gas giants orbiting within the star’s habitable zone. They have no solid surfaces, but large moons, if any exist, could in principle hold liquid water. The innermost planet, d, has about 6.7 Earth masses and may be rocky.

sections.title: ʻOumuamua’s possible birthplace
sections.text: Gliese 876 is a candidate home system for ʻOumuamua, the interstellar object that swept through the Solar System in 2017. Its path took it near the star about 820,000 years ago.

10pc-0096.name: L 143−23
10pc-0096.introduction: is a faint red dwarf about 15.8 light-years away, the nearest star in Carina. Like Proxima Centauri, it is an M5 dwarf with about 11% of the Sun’s mass, and at magnitude 13.9 it needs a telescope.

sections.title: A planet hint and a lookalike
sections.text: A 2007 study suggested a planet of about 2.4 Jupiter masses from tiny shifts in the star’s position. A faint background star passing close by could produce the same effect, so the planet remains unproven.

10pc-0097.name: GJ 1002
10pc-0097.introduction: is a quiet red dwarf about 15.8 light-years away in Cetus, also known as LHS 2. It hosts two Earth-mass planets in its habitable zone.

sections.title: Two temperate worlds
sections.text: Two planets announced in 2022 have minimum masses close to Earth’s, and both orbit within the habitable zone. As of 2023 they were the fourth- and fifth-closest known Earth-mass planets in a conservative habitable zone.

sections.title: A target for giant telescopes
sections.text: The planets do not transit, so their sizes are unknown. Because the star rotates slowly and is magnetically calm, future instruments such as the ANDES spectrograph on the Extremely Large Telescope may be able to detect their atmospheres.

10pc-0098.name: DENIS 0255−4700
10pc-0098.introduction: is the closest isolated L-type brown dwarf, about 15.9 light-years away in Eridanus. It is also the faintest brown dwarf with a measured visible magnitude.

sections.title: A day of 1.7 hours
sections.text: It spins once every 1.7 hours. At about 1,300 K, its atmosphere contains water vapor, methane and possibly ammonia. Its mass is uncertain, between 25 and 65 Jupiter masses, depending on its unknown age.

sections.title: Found by its color
sections.text: Xavier Delfosse singled it out in the DENIS survey by its very red color, and Keck spectra confirmed it in 1998. The RECONS team established its distance in 2006.

10pc-0099.name: Groombridge 1618
10pc-0099.introduction: is an orange dwarf about 15.9 light-years away in Ursa Major. At magnitude 6.6, it sits right at the edge of naked-eye visibility.

sections.title: An early parallax target
sections.text: It was entry 1618 in Stephen Groombridge’s catalog of circumpolar stars, published in 1838. Its large motion marked it as a near neighbor, and its parallax was measured by 1884, although that early value was too large.

sections.title: A cold dust ring
sections.text: Herschel observations suggest a faint ring of cold dust, below 22 K, at least 51 AU from the star. A planet claimed in 1989 was never confirmed and may have been caused by stellar activity.

sections.title: A “sweet spot” for life?
sections.text: With 67% of the Sun’s mass, it is one of five nearby K dwarfs that NASA’s Giada Arney placed in a “sweet spot” between Sun-like stars and red dwarfs for the chances of evolved life.

gj-412.name: Gliese 412
gj-412.introduction: is a wide pair of red dwarfs about 16 light-years away in Ursa Major, also called Lalande 21258. Its small companion, WX Ursae Majoris, is a flare star, and the pair belongs to the Milky Way’s old halo population.

sections.title: Argelander’s Third Star
sections.text: Friedrich Argelander announced its large proper motion in 1860, and Adalbert Krüger, who measured its parallax, called it Argelander’s Third Star.

sections.title: Mismatched partners
sections.text: A has 39% of the Sun’s mass and B less than 10%, about 150 AU apart. From B, A would look about as bright as a first-quarter Moon; from A, B would shine like Venus. B flares and emits X-rays, which were not detected from A. Adriaan van Maanen recorded one of its flares as early as 1939.

10pc-0102.name: AD Leonis
10pc-0102.introduction: is a young red dwarf about 16.2 light-years away in Leo, also called Gliese 388, and one of the most active flare stars known.

sections.title: A star covered in magnetism
sections.text: About 73% of its surface is covered by magnetically active regions, and X-ray observations show coronal loops reaching up to 30% of the star’s size, at around 6 million K. Only 25 to 300 million years old, it spins once every 2.2 days.

sections.title: Superflares
sections.text: Katherine Gordon and Gerald Kron first noticed its variability in 1949. Its flares have since been observed across the spectrum up to X-rays. In 2021, a superflare was recorded simultaneously in X-rays by XMM-Newton and in visible light by TESS.

sections.title: Rotation, not a planet
sections.text: A 2.23-day signal found in 2018 was briefly considered a possible giant planet. But the star rotates with the same period, and studies from 2020 onward attributed the signal to stellar activity.

10pc-0103.name: GJ 832
10pc-0103.introduction: is a red dwarf about 16.2 light-years away in Grus, orbited by a Jupiter-like planet on a decade-long orbit. Despite its flares, it gives off less ionizing radiation on average than the Sun.

sections.title: A Jupiter around a red dwarf
sections.text: Gliese 832 b was announced in 2008 after years of radial-velocity monitoring. Astrometry studies in 2023 and 2025 detected the star’s wobble across the sky, revealing a true mass close to Jupiter’s.

sections.title: The super-Earth that wasn’t
sections.text: GJ 832 c, announced in 2014 as a possible habitable-zone super-Earth, attracted wide attention. Its period turned out to be close to the star’s rotation period, and in 2022 the signal was attributed to stellar activity.

keid.name: 40 Eridani
keid.introduction: is a triple system about 16.3 light-years away in Eridanus: the orange dwarf Keid (A), the white dwarf B and the red dwarf C, also called DY Eridani. Keid is easy to see with the unaided eye, and B was the first white dwarf ever recognized.

sections.title: The first white dwarf
sections.text: William Herschel discovered the B–C pair in 1783. In 1910, astronomers realized that B was white yet very faint, so it had to be tiny: the first known white dwarf. It is still the easiest white dwarf to observe, nearly three magnitudes brighter than van Maanen’s Star and not lost in the glare of a bright partner.

sections.title: Three stars, three life stages
sections.text: B was once the most massive of the three, at about 1.8 solar masses, before it shed most of its mass. B and C orbit each other about 35 AU apart, roughly 400 AU from Keid. From a planet near Keid, B and C would shine at magnitudes −8 and −6, brighter than Venus appears from Earth.

sections.title: The real star behind Vulcan
sections.text: In Star Trek, Spock’s home planet Vulcan orbits 40 Eridani A. A planet candidate announced in 2018 with a 42-day orbit drew attention for that reason, but later studies traced the signal to the star’s own activity.

source.title: NASA: Spock’s home planet goes ‘poof’

sections.title: More fictional worlds
sections.text: Andy Weir’s Project Hail Mary places the planet Erid, home of the Eridian species, around 40 Eridani A, and in the Dune universe the star hosts the technological world Richese.

10pc-0106.name: GJ 682
10pc-0106.introduction: is a red dwarf about 16.3 light-years away in Scorpius, near the bright star Theta Scorpii. It lies in front of a crowded field toward the galactic center, only half a degree from the far more distant globular cluster NGC 6388.

sections.title: Planets lost, a giant suspected
sections.text: Two planets reported in 2014, one in the habitable zone, were not found by a 2020 study, which attributed the signals to stellar activity. In 2026, evidence emerged for a giant planet with a mass anywhere between 0.2 and 10 Jupiter masses, orbiting somewhere between 0.4 and 70 AU.

10pc-0112.name: EV Lacertae
10pc-0112.introduction: is a young, faint red dwarf about 16.5 light-years away, the nearest star in Lacerta. It produced the brightest flare ever seen from a star other than the Sun.

sections.title: A flare that triggered Swift
sections.text: On April 25, 2008, NASA’s Swift satellite detected an eruption thousands of times stronger than the largest observed solar flares. A star normally too faint for unaided viewing briefly became an extraordinary high-energy source.

source.title: NASA: Pipsqueak star unleashes monster flare

sections.title: Young, fast and magnetic
sections.text: At about 300 million years old, EV Lacertae still spins rapidly. Its fast rotation and convective interior drive a magnetic field much stronger than the Sun’s, which powers its exceptional flares.

ei-cancri.name: EI Cancri
ei-cancri.introduction: is a pair of very small red dwarfs about 16.7 light-years away in Cancer, also known as GJ 1116. Both lie at the very end of the main sequence, with surfaces cooler than 3,000 K.

sections.title: Five flares an hour
sections.text: In 1985, Bjørn Ragnvald Pettersen found that the system flares extremely often, averaging five flares per hour. It was named EI Cancri in 1987.

sections.title: A tight little binary
sections.text: The stars have about 13% and 11% of the Sun’s mass and orbit about 7 AU apart, taking an estimated 42 years.

msc-18055+0230.name: 70 Ophiuchi
msc-18055+0230.introduction: is a pair of orange dwarfs about 16.7 light-years away in Ophiuchus. At magnitude 4, it is visible to the unaided eye away from city lights.

sections.title: Proof that gravity is universal
sections.text: Ptolemy already listed it in the Almagest. In the late 18th century, William Herschel showed that its two stars orbit a common center, an important step in proving that Newton’s law of gravitation applies beyond the Solar System. They orbit every 88 years, between about 11 and 35 AU apart.

sections.title: The first exoplanet hunts
sections.text: In 1855, William Stephen Jacob claimed a “planetary body” disturbing the binary’s orbit, the first known attempt to find an exoplanet by astrometry. Further claims followed in 1899, 1932 and 1943, the last causing quite a sensation; all of them proved wrong.

10pc-0117.name: Altair
10pc-0117.introduction: is the twelfth-brightest star in the night sky, about 16.7 light-years away in Aquila, and one corner of the Summer Triangle. It spins so fast that it is visibly flattened, and it was the first main-sequence star other than the Sun to have its surface imaged.

sections.title: A star spinning near breakup
sections.text: Altair turns in under eight hours, faster than Jupiter or Saturn. Its equator moves at about 286 km/s, a large fraction of the roughly 400 km/s that would tear it apart, and its equatorial diameter is over 20% larger than its polar diameter.

sections.title: The first image of another star’s surface
sections.text: Because of its spin, Altair’s equator is cooler and dimmer than its poles, an effect called gravity darkening. Infrared observations with the CHARA array in 2006 produced an image of its surface, the first ever made of a main-sequence star other than the Sun.

sections.title: Young and pulsating
sections.text: With about 1.8 times the Sun’s mass and 11 times its luminosity, Altair is thought to be only about 100 million years old. Its brightness ripples by a few thousandths of a magnitude with periods under two hours, making it a Delta Scuti variable.

sections.title: The Cowherd and the Weaver Girl
sections.text: In Chinese legend, Altair is the cowherd Niulang, separated by the Milky Way from his wife Zhinü, the star Vega; magpies form a bridge so the two can meet once a year. Japan celebrates the story at the Tanabata festival. The name Altair comes from Arabic for “the flying eagle.”

10pc-0118.name: WISE 1506+7027
10pc-0118.introduction: is a T6 brown dwarf about 16.9 light-years away, the nearest known star or brown dwarf in Ursa Minor. Only a few brown dwarfs, including Luhman 16, WISE 0855−0714 and the Epsilon Indi pair, are closer.

sections.title: Closer, then farther
sections.text: Found in WISE data in 2011, it was first measured at about 11 light-years; Gaia later placed it at 16.9. Its large motion, about 1.6 arcseconds per year, explains why its survey names, based on positions at different dates, do not match exactly.

10pc-0119.name: G 99−49
10pc-0119.introduction: is a red dwarf about 17 light-years away, the nearest star in Orion, seen south-southeast of Betelgeuse. It is a foreground neighbor, unrelated to the distant bright stars that form Orion’s figure.

sections.title: A close pass in the past
sections.text: About 161,000 years ago it passed only about 4.1 light-years from the Sun, slightly closer than Proxima Centauri is today. It is now receding at 30 km/s.

sections.title: Fast spin, strong field
sections.text: It rotates every 1.8 days and has a magnetic field of about 2.3 kilogauss. Its brightness varies slightly as active regions turn into view.

10pc-0120.name: DENIS J0817−6155
10pc-0120.introduction: is a T6 brown dwarf about 17 light-years away in Carina, the brightest T dwarf in the sky in near-infrared light. It escaped notice until 2010 because it lies close to the crowded plane of the Milky Way.

sections.title: First detections of two molecules
sections.text: Gemini South spectra gave the first detections of molecular hydrogen and hydrogen sulfide in an atmosphere outside the Solar System, alongside methane, water vapor, carbon monoxide and ammonia. The hydrogen detection shows that its atmosphere is almost free of dust.

sections.title: Found by Étienne Artigau
sections.text: Étienne Artigau and colleagues reported it in 2010. It has a temperature of about 1,000 K and roughly 15 times Jupiter’s mass.

10pc-0121.name: Gliese 445
10pc-0121.introduction: is a red dwarf about 17.1 light-years away in Camelopardalis, rushing toward the Solar System. In about 40,000 years it will be one of the two nearest stars to the Sun.

sections.title: Voyager 1’s neighbor
sections.text: Voyager 1 will pass within about 1.6 light-years of Gliese 445 in about 40,000 years. By then the star will be only about 3.45 light-years from the Sun, roughly tied with Ross 248 as our closest stellar neighbor, yet still too faint to see with the naked eye.

10pc-0122.name: WISEA J1540−5101
10pc-0122.introduction: is a nearby late-M red dwarf in the southern constellation Norma, also designated WISEA J154045.67−510139.3.

source.title: Kirkpatrick et al. 2016: The AllWISE Motion Survey, Part 2

sections.title: A star found by its motion
sections.text: The AllWISE Motion Survey identified this previously overlooked neighbor in 2014. Follow-up spectra showed a cool M-type star, and later observations refined the optical classification to M6.5.

sections.title: WISE did not find only brown dwarfs
sections.text: Despite its WISE name, this object is a red dwarf rather than a T- or Y-type brown dwarf. Its discovery showed that even comparatively bright nearby infrared sources could still escape recognition in earlier surveys.

10pc-0123.name: 2MASS 0939−2448
10pc-0123.introduction: is probably a pair of cold T-type brown dwarfs about 17.4 light-years away in Antlia. From its discovery in 2005 until at least 2008, it was the dimmest brown dwarf known.

sections.title: Two objects in one point of light?
sections.text: A 2008 analysis found its luminosity and temperature hard to reconcile as one brown dwarf. Two unresolved objects, of perhaps 500 and 700 K, could explain the mismatch, although the two have not been seen separately and their individual properties depend on models.

source.title: Burgasser et al. 2008: A possible cold brown dwarf binary

sections.title: Clouds and possible auroras
sections.text: In 2025, Gemini South observations found small brightness changes repeating every 1.7 hours, likely caused by high-altitude clouds of compounds such as sodium sulfide or potassium chloride, or by auroral hot spots.

10pc-0124.name: GJ 3323
10pc-0124.introduction: is a red dwarf about 17.5 light-years away in Eridanus, also called LHS 1723, with a small planet on a five-day orbit. About 104,000 years ago it passed within 7.3 light-years of the Sun.

sections.title: Two planetary signals
sections.text: HARPS observations published in 2017 revealed two planets: b, with a year of only about five days, and c, which the discovery team considers a candidate.

10pc-0127.name: HD 119850
10pc-0127.introduction: is a red dwarf about 17.7 light-years away in Boötes, better known as Gliese 526 and also catalogued as Lalande 25372 and Wolf 498. It is a flare star that can brighten by 1 to 6 magnitudes.

sections.title: Two centuries of catalogs
sections.text: Jérôme Lalande listed it in his 1801 catalog. By 1911, Frank Schlesinger had measured its parallax and its large motion, and in 1919 Max Wolf added it to his catalog of fast-moving stars.

stein-2051.name: Stein 2051
stein-2051.introduction: is a wide pair about 18 light-years away in Camelopardalis: a red dwarf, A, and a white dwarf, B. It is the nearest separate red dwarf–white dwarf binary, and B was the first white dwarf weighed by the way it bends starlight. B is the more massive star, yet A is brighter.

sections.title: Weighed by gravity’s lens
sections.text: In 2014, Stein 2051 B passed close to a distant background star on the sky. Hubble measured how B’s gravity shifted that star’s apparent position, and the analysis published in 2017 gave B a mass of about 0.675 solar masses.

source.title: Sahu et al. 2017: Relativistic deflection measures a white dwarf’s mass

sections.title: A puzzle resolved
sections.text: Earlier, uncertain orbital estimates had suggested an unusual iron-core white dwarf. The lensing mass instead fits an ordinary carbon–oxygen core and the expected relation between a white dwarf’s mass and radius.

10pc-0130.name: 2MASS 1114−2618
10pc-0130.introduction: is a late-T brown dwarf about 17.6 light-years away in Hydra, found in 2005 in a 2MASS search for methane-bearing brown dwarfs.

sections.title: A fast-moving neighbor
sections.text: It crosses about 3 arcseconds of sky each year, corresponding to about 78 km/s across our line of sight. Its distance was first estimated at about 23 light-years; a parallax measured in 2026 brought it to 17.6.

10pc-0131.name: Wolf 294
10pc-0131.introduction: is a red dwarf about 18.2 light-years away, the nearest star in Gemini, also known as Gliese 251. A super-Earth in its habitable zone, announced in 2025, could be a target for the next generation of telescopes.

sections.title: A planetary picture that changed
sections.text: Two candidates proposed in 2019 turned out in 2020 to be stellar activity. The same CARMENES data revealed a real super-Earth, GJ 251 b, on a 14-day orbit.

sections.title: A temperate super-Earth
sections.text: In 2025, a second super-Earth, GJ 251 c, was reported on a roughly 54-day orbit in the star’s habitable zone. Its proximity makes it a candidate for direct imaging with next-generation telescopes; its radius and surface conditions are still unknown.

source.title: Beard et al. 2025: A nearby habitable-zone super-Earth candidate

10pc-0133.name: LP 816−60
10pc-0133.introduction: is a single red dwarf about 18.3 light-years away in Capricornus. Its name comes from Willem Luyten’s Palomar proper-motion surveys.

sections.title: A Sun-like magnetic cycle
sections.text: Its starspots wax and wane over a cycle of about 10.6 years, close to the length of the Sun’s 11-year cycle.

10pc-0134.name: WISE 0350−5658
10pc-0134.introduction: is a very cold Y1 brown dwarf about 18.5 light-years away, the nearest known star or brown dwarf in Reticulum. At about 350 K, roughly 75 °C, it is about as warm as a cup of hot tea.

sections.title: A possible rogue planet
sections.text: Estimates put its mass between about 3 and 13 Jupiter masses. Its low speed and possibly high metal content hint that it is young, in which case it could be a free-floating planet rather than a brown dwarf.

sections.title: Chemistry out of balance
sections.text: J. Davy Kirkpatrick and colleagues discovered it in WISE data in 2012. Gemini spectra are matched better by models in which gas is stirred up and down faster than its chemistry can settle than by models in chemical equilibrium.

10pc-0135.name: LSR J1835+3259
10pc-0135.introduction: is an ultracool dwarf about 18.5 light-years away in Lyra, near the boundary between the smallest stars and brown dwarfs. It was the first object beyond the Solar System where auroras were detected.

sections.title: Auroras a million times brighter
sections.text: In 2015, radio observations with the Very Large Array revealed auroras probably about a million times brighter than any seen on Earth. The optical glow is mainly red, from charged particles striking hydrogen. Their cause is unknown; one idea is an unseen planet or moon feeding material to its magnetic field, as Io does for Jupiter.

sections.title: The first radiation belt beyond the Solar System
sections.text: In 2023, astronomers used 39 coordinated radio dishes to image a double-lobed radiation belt around it, the first observed outside the Solar System. It resembles Jupiter’s belts but would be about 10 million times brighter.

source.title: UC Santa Cruz: First radiation belt observed outside the Solar System

10pc-0136.name: HD 36395
10pc-0136.introduction: is a red dwarf about 18.6 light-years away in Orion, also called Gliese 205. Friedrich Bessel’s observers at Königsberg probably recorded it as early as January 8, 1823.

sections.title: Planet candidates that faded
sections.text: Two Neptune-mass candidates with 17- and 270-day orbits were proposed in a 2019 preprint. A 2023 study found no evidence for them and measured a stellar rotation period of 34.4 days, showing how the star’s own activity can mimic planets.

10pc-0137.name: 2MASS 0415−0935
10pc-0137.introduction: is a cold T8 brown dwarf about 18.6 light-years away in Eridanus, with a temperature of about 750 K. It is the reference object that defines the T8 spectral class.

sections.title: Setting the standard
sections.text: Adam Burgasser and colleagues discovered it in 2002 in the same study that defined T subtypes T1 to T8. Their 11 new T dwarfs nearly doubled the number then known.

sections.title: Missing phosphine
sections.text: Webb measured water vapor, methane, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide and ammonia in its atmosphere but found no phosphine. Together with other cold brown dwarfs lacking phosphine, this calls for a major revision of phosphorus chemistry in brown dwarfs and possibly giant planets.

gj-229.name: Gliese 229
gj-229.introduction: is a red dwarf about 18.8 light-years away, the nearest star system in Lepus. Its companion, Gliese 229 B, was one of the first brown dwarfs ever discovered, and in 2024 it turned out to be two.

sections.title: The first methane brown dwarf
sections.text: Found in 1994 and confirmed in 1995, Gliese 229 B showed methane in its spectrum, clear evidence of an object far too cold to be a star. It became the prototype of the T dwarfs and helped establish brown dwarfs as a real population between stars and planets.

sections.title: The famous companion was twins
sections.text: For decades, B seemed too faint for its mass. Observations reported in 2024 resolved the puzzle: Ba and Bb orbit each other about every 12 days, only about 16 times the Earth–Moon distance apart. Their combined light had been mistaken for one object for nearly three decades.

source.title: Caltech: It’s twins! Mystery of famed brown dwarf solved

sections.title: Made from the same material
sections.text: Webb mid-infrared spectra show that both brown dwarfs share the red dwarf’s carbon-to-oxygen ratio and heavy-element content, consistent with the three forming together.
